statements.text: AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI.
statements.venue: Press release on Great American AI Act discussion draft (Trahan/Obernolte)

statements.text: But our community is paying the price now. [...] And one can support an innovation, but it does not have to come at the cost of our com- munities.
statements.context: Speaking at a congressional hearing titled "America's AI Moonshot: The Economics of AI, Data Centers, and Power Consumption," Rep. Subramanyam recounts the local impacts of data-center concentration in his Virginia district.

statements.text: I think we have some good ideas that we can maybe turn into legislation, and we can hopefully make sure that we empower bases to both have the right technologies to address this, as well as to make sure more military installations are covered under stat- ute potentially, make sure there is better coordination with state, local, and Federal, and make sure that overall we have a workforce and the capacity to be able to address these challenges.
statements.context: Closing remarks at a House Subcommittee hearing on unauthorized drone activity over U.S. military installations.

statements.text: And so, we have heard a lot about this already from people testifying and even from Members here, that it is not just about having AI, it is about having to deploy AI in a responsible way and in a manner in which we are not letting AI make mistakes. I will give you an example. In Michigan about, let us say, 10 years ago now, they deployed AI to try to find fraud, and they ended up finding a lot of fraud where there was not any fraud. [...] then they realized that the AI had made a big mistake.
statements.context: Speaking at a House Oversight subcommittee hearing titled "The Federal Government in the Age of Artificial Intelligence."

statements.text: what jobs are we going to lose in the future as well? [...] Do we even know right now what those jobs would be?
statements.context: A lawmaker questions expert witnesses at a congressional hearing on the future of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: If you could replace 100 people that you spend a million dollars paying with a tool that costs $50,000, it is part of your mandate to do that [...] we have invested a lot already in STEM education and in job training programs.
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing titled 'Shaping Tomorrow: The Future of Artificial Intelligence', closing remarks by a committee member.

statements.text: But now we are seeing it at a different level. We are seeing companies now, basically, lay off entire depart- ments and replace them with AI.
statements.context: Rep. Subramanyam questions witnesses at a congressional hearing titled "Shaping Tomorrow: The Future of Artificial Intelligence."

statements.text: I want people to understand that we should not downplay the job losses, the job displacement that is already happening. [...] And then I look at what is happening at the companies, and they are laying off entire departments and replacing them with AI [...] I do want to work with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to figure out what comes next [...]
statements.context: Rep. Subramanyam speaking at a House committee hearing on the future of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: I would ask all the witnesses what should Congress do, if anything, about job displacement? [...] I think investing in workforce development and training and apprenticeships. [...] continuing to invest in upskilling is extremely important.
statements.context: House hearing titled “Shaping Tomorrow: The Future of Artificial Intelligence,” where Representative Subramanyam questions industry witnesses on AI-driven job loss.

statements.text: We are seeing companies now, basically, lay off entire departments and replace them with AI. [...] But it is creating a problem that Congress has to figure out how to address, which is jobs, because one thing we want is jobs available for people. We have been telling people—we have been telling kids for to the past 10 or 15 years, go into STEM, right, learn to code, like, that is going to be your meal ticket. You can have a job for 30 years being a coder, an engineer. And now we have AI that can do their job.
statements.context: Rep. Subramanyam questions witnesses at a congressional hearing on the future of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: And I've been working on, AI safety and AI, sort of the risks and how to mitigate these risks, for a long time.
statements.context: Verbatim transcript of a congressional discussion on America's AI Action Plan, with Mr. Subramanyam asking a witness about the federal government's role in AI risk mitigation.

statements.text: I think we are all in agreement that small businesses should be able to take advantage of the immense potential of AI as well as be able to understand the risks and cybersecurity pitfalls that may come out of it.
statements.context: Floor remarks in the U.S. House of Representatives urging passage of the Small Business Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act (H.R. 3679).

statements.text: This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to establish and distribute resources on how small businesses can adopt AI tools and risk management practices.
statements.context: Floor remarks in the House of Representatives advocating for a bill directing NIST to support small business AI adoption.

statements.text: That is why I am introducing this week the small AI innovators empowerment act. [...] This bill would look at challenges that small AI businesses and startups face, including areas like access to funding, hiring and retention of talented employees, and the impact of regulatory uncertainty.
statements.context: Floor remarks in the U.S. House of Representatives announcing a new bill to support small AI businesses and startups.

statements.text: The reality is if we want to grow and develop some of these emerging technologies like AI and others, we will need more data storage and data centers is a part of that. What we don't need is data centers to be steamrolling communities and being put in places that don't want them. [...] People talk about the issue with China, but honestly people who are seeing their utility bills double and triple don't care about the race against China. We're gonna lose that race, because 70% of Americans now don't want data centers in their community.

There's a lot of things that we're trying to fine-tune in the bill, and we're going to be working on that in September. A lot of what we're doing in the bill is encouraging third parties to be involved with the companies along the way, to make sure there's containment in place. It's assumed in the bill that we're going to be doing a lot on containment, but one of the things I'm going to be working on is trying to see if we can get explicit containment prescription guidelines in the bill to do that.

I'm hoping that by the end of the year … we, as a Congress and as a federal government, have at least worked towards solving the big concern about an AI model getting out and going a little crazy and doing a lot of harm to a lot of people.

Mr. Speaker, I sat down with some of the leaders in the AI industry. They told me that there were going to be dire consequences if we didn't put AI safeguards in place and that there would be massive implications for our country and for the world if we didn't act. [...] We have AI frontier models with the capability to wreak havoc. We are getting to a place where AI can self-improve and duplicate itself. The stuff that was theoretical 10 years ago is now happening. We have swarms of AI chatbots working together in a Machiavellian way to hack and undermine systems.

There are commonsense ways that security researchers, industry experts, and even Members of Congress here agree can make this safer, like auditing, information reporting, transparency, building safety throughout the AI development process, and real containment strategies, so that AI models don't escape their sandbox during development. [...] It is because voluntary standards are not a true safeguard, and sitting on the sidelines is not a safeguard.
